rows.answer:
For a discussion group, the core is the four-part argument against computational functionalism, the idea that the right computation is enough for consciousness. It starts at "First, and most important, brains are not computers" [spya-a8jgf4]. You can skim the Turing and McCulloch-Pitts history [spya-cf70dt] and the figure captions, since the technical detail isn't what the argument turns on. Then read the section on why life might matter [spya-hj5y6s] and the one on simulation versus instantiation [spya-npjt4j] more slowly. Your group will probably argue about those two.

Your history-of-science eye may like his habit of treating "brain as computer" as a metaphor [spya-uwxe4h].

offers.text: My partner keeps saying chatbots are conscious and I want ammunition to argue back.

rows.answer:
You can save that reason with the button under this answer.

Go straight to the four arguments, which start at "Brains Are Not Computers" [spya-sk4su6]. The sharpest single point for a debate is that "simulation is not instantiation" [spya-cqh5wq]. A simulated rainstorm doesn't make anything wet. Before you argue, read the section on our biases [spya-cvaqgs], because it explains why a chatbot feels conscious even when it isn't. Seth also concedes he might be wrong [spya-qu7j89], so he's no use for claiming certainty.

Quotes would give you the lines worth quoting back.
